```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
hood = readRDS("data/2010-2024_sacramento_river_hood_water_temp.rds")
```

# Time Series

::: {.callout-note title="Learning Goals" collapse="false"}
After this lesson, you should be able to:

* Summarize the current ecosystem of R packages for time series
* Explain the primary concerns when cleaning a time series
* Plot time series
* Explain what trend, seasonal, and remainder components are
* Explain what cycles are
* Use seasonality plots to check for seasonality
* Use STL decomposition to extract components of a time series
* Explain how to assess the quality of an STL decomposition
* Explain what autocorrelations and partial autocorrelations are
* Use autocorrelation plots to assess trend and seasonality in time series
* Explain what it means for a time series to be stationary
* Describe some simple methods for forecasting
* Fit a linear model to a time series and use it to forecast
* Fit an ARIMA model to a time series and use it to forecast
* Explain some ways to assess the quality of a fitted time series model
:::

:::{.callout-important title="Required Packages"}
This chapter uses the following R packages:

* dplyr
* fable
* feasts
* forecast
* ggplot2
* ggtime
* lubridate
* tsibble

For a refresher about how to install and load packages, see the
[Packages][r-basics-packages] section of DataLab's R Basics workshop reader.

[r-basics-packages]: https://ucdavisdatalab.github.io/dwr_workshop_r_basics/chapters/getting-started/getting-started.html#sec-packages
:::

This chapter introduces the fundamentals of time series analysis. Time series
analysis is a deep topic and remains an area of active research, so this
chapter should not be considered comprehensive by any means.


## Time Series in R {#sec-ts-time-series-r}

There are many different packages and data structures for representing time
series in R. A few of these include:

* R's built-in time series (see `?ts`)
* The [forecast][] package (after installing, see `?msts`)
* The [tsibble][] package (after installing, see `?tsibble`)
* The [zoo][] package (after installing, see `?zoo` and `?zooreg`)
* The [xts][] package (after installing, see `?xts`)

[forecast]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.forecast
[tsibble]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.tsibble
[zoo]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.zoo
[xts]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.xts

Unfortunately, these representations are mostly incompatible with each other
(but see the [tsbox][] package, which provides conversion functions). Which
representations are supported by methods packages varies.

[tsbox]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.tsbox

In this reader, we mostly use tsibble (and associated packages) to so that
learners can easily refer to the textbook [_Forecasting: Principles and
Practice_, 3rd Edition][fpp3] [@hyndman2021]. We've found that tsibbles lead to
the nicest visualizations (with good ggplot2 support) and are also the most
convenient for time series with multiple features (sometimes called
multivariate time series or panel data).

[fpp3]: https://otexts.com/fpp3/

We may occasionally use forecast as well. It's an older package from several of
the same developers as tsibble; visualizations aside, it generally has more
features, better performance, and fewer bugs. The textbook [_Forecasting:
Principles and Practice_, 2nd Editon][fpp2] [@hyndman2018] provides an
introduction to the forecast package.

[fpp2]: https://otexts.com/fpp2/

:::{.callout-note title="See Also"}
The [CRAN Task View: Time Series Analysis][cran-ts] page is a curated list of
R's most prominent time series packages.

The [Time Series Analysis][rcook-ts] chapter of the _R Cookbook_ [@long2019]
discusses the tradeoffs of R's many time series data structures (and recommends
zoo or xts for most purposes). It also provides examples of several common time
series analysis tasks.

[cran-ts]: https://cran.r-project.org/web/views/TimeSeries.html
[rcook-ts]: https://rc2e.com/timeseriesanalysis
:::


## Cleaning {#sec-ts-cleaning}

As with any dataset, the first step in working with a time series is to clean
it. Specifically, we need to:

* Identify outliers. Later in this section, we'll explain some strategies
  tailored to time series, but most general-purpose strategies (@sec-outliers)
  are also appropriate. If there are outliers, we need to investigate further
  to decide whether they're valid (and should be left as-is) or erroneous (and
  should be corrected or removed).

* Check for missing values. If there are missing values, determine how many and
  whether they exhibit any patterns. We'll introduce a few ways to impute
  missing values later in this section.

* Check whether the series is **regular**, meaning the interval of time between
  each pair of consecutive observations is the same. A series that's not
  regular is **irregular**. Many time series methods assume regularity, so
  working with an irregular series is often difficult. Fortunately, there are
  several ways to regularize an irregular series, such as "rounding" times,
  aggregating to a coarser timescale, or interpolating the missing
  "observations" on a regular grid.

* Check for "gaps" in the series. This is related to checking for missing
  values and regularity, but gaps can also arise due to missing observations
  (that is, observations which are not present in the dataset). When a series
  has a long interval with relatively few or no observations, it may be better
  to treat it as two separate series. Consider whether each (separate) part of
  the series contains uniquely important information relevant to the analysis.
  For forecasting, we often focus the most on relatively recent observations.

To illustrate some of these points, let's clean the Sacramento Water
Temperature dataset (@sec-dataset-sac-water-temp). To check for outliers, let's
start by visualizing the dataset. For time series, it's natural to make point
or line plots of numerical features against time. In this dataset, the only
numerical feature is `temp_f`, the water temperature in degrees Fahrenheit:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-line-messy
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Line plot of time versus temperature for the Sacramento River Water
#|    Temperature dataset.
library("ggplot2")

ggplot(hood) +
  aes(x = time, y = temp_f) +
  geom_line()
```

The most striking thing in @fig-sacwt-line-messy is that at least two of the
temperatures are close to 10,000! These are clearly either erroneous or meant
to indicate the the actual measurement is missing.

It's reasonable to expect that the water temperature will never be below
freezing (32°F; it's extremely rare for the Sacramento River to freeze) or
above boiling (212°F). Let's check how many observations are outside these
bounds:

```{r}
#| warning: false
library("dplyr")

print(filter(hood, temp_f < 32 | temp_f > 212), n = 30)
```

All of these are either 14 or 9,999. Both seem unlikely to be valid
measurements, so let's replace these with missing values, then replot the
series:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-line
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Line plot of time versus temperature for the Sacramento River Water
#|    Temperature dataset, after removing temperatures below freezing and above
#|    boiling.
hood$temp_f[hood$temp_f < 32 | hood$temp_f > 212] = NA

ggplot(hood) +
  aes(x = time, y = temp_f) +
  geom_line()
```

@fig-sacwt-line shows there is a strong, wavelike pattern to the temperatures
over time. This likely reflects changes in season. There are still about three
observations that seem to deviate substantially from the others; their values
are extremely unlikely but not impossible, so we'll leave them as-is for now.
The figure also shows that there are no major gaps in the series.

Next, let's check whether the series is regular. To do this, we'll use the
[tsibble][] package, which provides a Tidyverse-compatible data structure for
time series: a "time series tibble" or tsibble. To convert the data frame, we
can use the `tsibble` function; we also need to specify which feature is the
time index for the series:

```{r}
library("tsibble")

hood = tsibble(hood, index = time)
```

After converting the series, we can use the `scan_gaps` function to identify
missing observations (and gaps):

```{r}
scan_gaps(hood)
```

The series is mostly regular, but there are 15 times for which there's no
observation. We can use tsibble's `fill_gaps` function to insert observations
at these times (with missing values for the features):

```{r}
hood = fill_gaps(hood)
```

:::{.callout-tip}
Another way to check regularity is to compute differences between observation
times with R's built in `diff` function. In a regular series, the differences
will all be equal.

Another way to insert missing observations is to use `seq` to create a regular
sequence of times, then use `merge` or dplyr's `left_join` to left join the
sequence with the time series.
:::

Finally, let's check for missing values in the time series:

```{r}
summary(hood)
```

There are `r sum(is.na(hood$temp_f))` missing values (39 of which we created)
out of `r nrow(hood)` observations. Let's create a new column to mark the
observations where temperature is missing:

```{r}
hood$na_temp = is.na(hood$temp_f)
```

Since temperature is only missing for a small proportion of observations, let's
impute the missing values. There are many different ways to do this. For
instance, we can propagate prior non-missing values forward, aggregate the
nearest non-missing values, or fit a model to the non-missing values and use
its predictions.

The [forecast][] package's `na.interp` function can impute missing values in a
vector or time series by linear interpolation:

```{r}
library("forecast")

hood$temp_f = as.numeric(na.interp(hood$temp_f, linear = TRUE))
```

The argument `linear = TRUE` makes the function use linear interpolation; it
can also impute values by time series decomposition (more about this in
@sec-ts-decomposition). The function returns a `ts` object, so we also need to
convert it back to a vector with `as.numeric`.

Now that we've imputed the missing values, we can plot the series one more time
with the imputed values marked. This is one way to check for patterns in (the
former) missing values:


```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-line-na
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Line plot of time versus temperature for the Sacramento River Water
#|    Temperature dataset, with imputed values marked in red.
ggplot(hood) +
  aes(x = time, y = temp_f) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = filter(hood, na_temp), color = "red", size = 0.1)
```

Based on @fig-sacwt-line-na, the former missing values are relatively spread
out across the series. There appear to be a few clusters of missing values,
which could indicate a multi-hour sensor failure. We'll proceed with the
imputed values. In practice, we should carry out further investigation of the
missing values to look for patterns, identify potential causes, and evaluate
how they might influence subsequent analyses. However, since the number of
missing values was small, and this series includes a large number of
observations, they're unlikely to have much impact.


## Decomposition {#sec-ts-decomposition}

Many time series can be decomposed into meaningful components:

* A **trend** component: a smooth curve that follows long-term increases and
  decreases in the series. Some time series also exhibit long-term **cycles**:
  patterns of increases and decreases over irregular lengths of time. When a
  series has cycles, we call this a **trend-cycle** component.

* One or more **seasonal** components: a curve which follows increases and
  decreases that repeat over a fixed (or regular) length of time. We call the
  fixed length of time a **seasonal period** or simply a season. There can be
  multiple seasonal components with different season lengths---we'll see an
  example of this shortly.

* A **remainder** component: the variation in the observations that's left over
  after removing the trend and seasonal components. Generally, we want this
  component to be devoid of any trends, cycles, or seasonal patterns.

There are many different methods for decomposing time series.


### Seasonality Plots {#sec-ts-seasonality-plots}

As a first step towards decomposition, let's make a **seasonality plot**. In a
seasonality plot, we split the time series into subseries by season, align each
subseries to the same starting time, and then make a time versus feature plot
with a separate line for each subseries. The idea is that any seasonal patterns
will be visible in the plot as similarities between in the subseries.

The [ggtime][] package provides functions to make seasonality plots for
tsibbles. It also provides functions for other kinds of time series
visualizations. The package is relatively new as of writing, so there are some
missing features and bugs.

[ggtime]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.ggtime

The ggtime function to make a seasonality plot is `gg_season`. The function
requires three arguments: a tsibble, the name of the feature to plot on the
y-axis, and the seasonal period. See `?gg_season` for details about how to set
the seasonal period; stricly speaking, this argument is optional, but it's
usually best to specify it.

Let's make a seasonality plot where the seasonal period is one year for the
Sacramento River Water Temperature series:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-season-year
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Seasonality plot with a 1-year seasonal period for the Sacramento River
#|    Water Temperature dataset.
library("ggtime")

gg_season(hood, temp_f, "1y")
```

There's a clear pattern visible in @fig-sacwt-season-year. At the beginning of
the year, in Winter, temperatures are relatively low (about 50°F). They
gradually increase over time until the peak in Summer (about 70°F). Then they
gradually decrease as Winter approaches again. So this series has strong
seasonality at the 1-year level; any decomposition we make should include a
1-year seasonal component.

It's up to us to determine appropriate seasonal period(s) for a time series
(although some functions will try to guess). In general, we should check the
seasonality plots for any seasonal periods that we suspect might exhibit a
pattern, regardless of whether that's because we have expert knowledege about
the processes that affect the series or because we see signs of the pattern in
the initial time versus feature plots.

Let's check the 1-month and 1-week seasonality plots:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-season-month
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Seasonality plot with a 1-month seasonal period for the Sacramento River
#|    Water Temperature dataset.
gg_season(hood, temp_f, "1m")
```

In @fig-sacwt-season-month, it's much harder to see a clear pattern than it was
in @fig-sacwt-season-year. One notable pattern is that there are small bumps
over the course of the entire month; these suggest there might be seasonality
over a shorter seasonal period.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-season-week
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Seasonality plot with a 1-week seasonal period for the Sacramento River
#|    Water Temperature dataset.
gg_season(hood, temp_f, "1w")
```

@fig-sacwt-season-week doesn't exhibit any strong week-level patterns, but once
again there are small bumps. They appear to correspond to days (there are seven
bumps), so let's check the 1-day seasonality plot:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-season-day
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Seasonality plot with a 1-day seasonal period for the Sacramento River
#|    Water Temperature dataset.
gg_season(hood, temp_f, "1d")
```

The annual seasonality we saw in @fig-sacwt-season-year makes it quite
difficult to see patterns in the 1-day seasonality plot in
@fig-sacwt-season-day. The 1-day seasonality was easier to see in
@fig-sacwt-season-week. Based on what we know about earth, it seems likely that
temperatures increase during the day and decrease at night.

After reviewing the seasonality plots for the Sacramento River Water
Temperature series, we can conclude that there are seasonal effects at the
1-year and 1-day level. When we decompose the series, we should compute
seasonal components at both of these levels.

:::{.callout-tip}
The ggtime package's `autoplot` function is a convenient way to make a time
versus feature plot for a tsibble:

```{r}
autoplot(hood, temp_f)
```

This is the same as @fig-sacwt-line, but the code is much more concise. The
`autoplot` function returns an ordinary ggplot2 object, so we can still add
layers to customize the plot.
:::


### STL Decomposition {#sec-ts-stl-decomposition}

The Seasonal-Trend Decomposition Procedure Based on LOESS [@cleveland1990],
commonly known as **STL**, is a very effective method for decomposing time
series. An STL decomposition provides numerical estimates of the trend and
seasonal components for a series.

The core of STL is a 2-step process:

1. Fit a seasonal component after removing the trend component.
2. Fit a trend component after removing the seasonal component.

These steps are repeated many times, starting from an initial trend component
of 0 (no trend). STL uses **LOESS** ("locally estimated scatterplot
smoothing"), a kind of local polynomial regression, to fit each component.
Local polynomial regression approximates a smooth curve by fitting a polynomial
(via least squares) at each point where the curve is to be evaluated. STL also
uses some additional steps to handle spikes in series robustly; see
@cleveland1990 for details.

In R, the [feasts][] package provides an implementation of STL that works with
tsibbles. To fit an STL decomposition, we can use the package's `model`
function, which is a generic interface for fitting models. The first argument
must be the time series to decompose. The second argument must be a model
description.

[feasts]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.feasts

For an STL decomposition, we can use the `STL` function to write the model
description. The function's only required argument is a model formula, written
with `~`, which describes the decomposition. The left-hand side should be the
feature to decompose. On the right-hand side, we can use the `trend` and
`season` functions to describe which components to extract.

:::{.callout-tip}
An STL decomposition always includes a trend component, so we can omit the
`trend` function in the model description unless we want to set parameters
related to the trend.

See `?STL` for more details.
:::

As a demonstration, let's apply STL decomposition to the Sacramento River Water
Temperature series. We'll extract seasonal components at the 1-year and 1-day
level, since we saw patterns there in @sec-ts-seasonality-plots. The code to
fit the STL decomposition is:

```{r}
library("feasts")

stl_fit = model(
  hood,
  STL(
    temp_f ~ season("1y") + season("1d"),
    robust = TRUE  # make fit robust against outliers
  )
)
```

After fitting an STL decomposition, we'll generally want to inspect or use the
individual components. We can get the components as a tsibble with the
`components` function:

```{r}
stl_cmp = components(stl_fit)
stl_cmp
```

The result includes columns for the original series, the trend component
(`trend`), each seasonal component (`season_*`), and the remainder
(`remainder`) after removing the trend and seasonal components from the series.
It also includes a column for the **seasonally adjusted** series
(`season_adjust`), which is the series with only the seasonal components
removed. The seasonally adjusted series is useful when we're only interested in
trend or want to use a forecasting method that assumes no seasonality.

The best way to inspect an STL decomposition is by plotting it. The ggtime
package's `autoplot` function automatically makes a per-component plot for STL
components:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-stl
#| fig-cap: >
#|    STL components plot for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.
autoplot(stl_cmp)
```

From top to bottom, @fig-sacwt-stl shows the original series, the trend
component, the seasonal components, and the remainder. At the left-hand side of
each panel, a gray bar shows the relative scale of the component: each gray bar
has the same height in the units of the original time series.

The STL decomposition for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series shows
a mostly flat trend (compare the heights of the gray bars in the panel for the
original series and the trend component). The 1-year seasonal component has a
parabolic shape, similar to the pattern in @fig-sacwt-season-year.

By default, STL allows seasonal components to change slowly from one season to
the next. @fig-sacwt-stl suggests that this has caused some of the 1-year
seasonal component to leak into the 1-day seasonal component---notice how the
peaks in the 1-year and 1-day seasonal components are similar. The 1-day
seasonal component also appears as a filled area instead of a curve because it
fluctuates over hours, but the plot is on the scale of years. We can plot the
1-day component separately over a shorter time interval, say the first week of
January 2024, to make patterns easier to see:

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-sacwt-stl-day
#| fig-cap: >
#|    1-day seasonal STL component plot for the Sacramento River Water
#|    Temperature dataset, limited to the first week of January 2024.
library("lubridate")
# Limit from 2024-01-01 to 2024-01-07.
lims = make_datetime(year = 2024, month = 1, day = c(1, 7))

autoplot(stl_cmp, season_1d) +
  xlim(lims)
```

@fig-sacwt-stl-day reveals the pattern for each day and also shows how it's
slowly changing.

:::{.callout-warning}
The ggplot2 package sometimes converts datetimes into dates, which can make
hourly plots like @fig-sacwt-stl-day visually misleading.

One way to ensure that a plot uses datetimes is to explicitly set the limits in
terms of datetimes (not dates!), as we did for the figure.
:::

For series where there are multiple seasonal components and the largest one
leaks into the others, it can be useful to disallow gradual change for the
smaller seasonal components. To do so, we refit the STL model with the setting
`window = "periodic"` for the seasonal components where we want to disallow
change:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-stl-periodic
#| fig-cap: >
#|    STL components plot for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset,
#|    with periodic 1-day seasonal component.
stl_fit = model(
  hood,
  STL(
    temp_f ~ season("1y") + season("1d", window = "periodic"),
    robust = TRUE  # make fit robust against outliers
  )
)

stl_cmp = components(stl_fit)

autoplot(stl_cmp)
```

In @fig-sacwt-stl-periodic, the trend and 1-year seasonal components look about
the same as with the previous model. The 1-day seasonal component looks like a
black rectangle, again because it fluctuates over hours and the plot is on the
scale of years. We can see the 1-day seasonal component better by focusing on a
single week:

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-sacwt-stl-periodic-day
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Periodic 1-day seasonal STL component plot for the Sacramento River Water
#|    Temperature dataset, limited to the first week of January 2024.
autoplot(stl_cmp, season_1d) +
  xlim(lims)
```

@fig-sacwt-stl-periodic-day shows that starting from midnight each day,
temperatures decrease until about 6 am, then increase until about 6 pm, then
decrease again. The overall change in temperature is relatively small (less
than 1°F).

:::{.callout-note title="Note: STL Parameters"}
There are several parameters that can be adjusted in the STL decomposition. The
automatic decomposition we used here is not necessarily the best one.

To learn more about these parameters, see `?STL` and @cleveland1990.
:::

:::{.callout-note title="Note: Multiplicative Decompositions"}
Throughout this section, we've assumed that decompositions are **additive**:
adding up the trend, seasonal, and remainder components gives the original
series.

For a positive time series where the variations increase and decrease with the
level of the series, it often makes more sense to use a **multiplicative**
decomposition. In this case, multiplying the components gives the original
series.

One way to achieve a multiplicative decomposition is to take logarithms of the
series before decomposition. There are also decomposition methods that are
specifically multiplicative (or have both additive and multiplicative
versions).
:::

:::{.callout-note title="See Also"}
There are several other methods for decomposing time series, ranging from
simple to extremely complicated. Time series decomposition is often of interest
to government agencies, so many of the methods have been developed by
statisticians working for the United States and other countries. To learn more
about these, see the [Time Series Decomposition][fpp-decomp] chapter of
_Forecasting: Principles and Practice_, 3rd edition [@hyndman2021].

[fpp-decomp]: https://otexts.com/fpp3/decomposition.html
:::

c(
  trend = var(stl_cmp$trend),
  season_1y = var(stl_cmp$season_1y),
  season_1d = var(stl_cmp$season_1d),
  remainder = var(stl_cmp$remainder)
) / var(stl_cmp$temp_f)
-->


## Autocorrelations

One more statistic we can use (and visualize) to investigate a series is
**autocorrelation**. Autocorrelation is the correlation (@sec-correlation)
between a time series and a time-lagged version of the same time series. For
instance, lag-1 autocorrelation is the correlation between the series and the
series lagged (shifted back) by 1 time step. As correlations, autocorrelations
are bounded between -1 and 1, with 0 indicating no relationship and -1 or 1
indicating a strong negative or positive relationship.

In practical terms, large lag-1 autocorrelation means that we can effectively
predict an observation with the previous observation. Large lag-2
autocorrelation means there's useful predictive information 2 observations
back, and so on.

The `ACF` function in the feasts package computes autocorrelations for a
tsibble. The first two arguments are the time series and feature, respectively.
We can optionally set the `lag_max` parameter to specify how many
autocorrelations to compute.

Let's compute autocorrelations for the Sacramento River Water Temperature
series:

```{r}
hood_acf = ACF(hood, temp_f, lag_max = 24*5)
head(hood_acf)
```

We can use the `autoplot` function to make an **autocorrelation plot**, which
shows lags on the x-axis and autocorrelations on the y-axis:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-acf
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Autocorrelation plot for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.
autoplot(hood_acf)
```

The autocorrelation plot shows two dashed horizontal lines at the upper and
lower bounds for a significance test of zero autocorrelation. The test can be
helpful for identifying which autocorrelations are likely to be zero. However,
for a time series with a large number of observations, the bounds will be very
close to zero, so even negligible autocorrelations will be considered
statistically discernible. Thus it's important to consider the actual
autocorrelation value (the effect size) in addition to discernibility.

:::{.callout-tip}
When a time series has a trend, the autocorrelations tend to be large at low
lags and decrease slowly as the number of lags increases.

When a time series has seasonality, the largest autocorrelations tend to be at
lags that are multiples of the seasonal period.
:::

The autocorrelations for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series exhibit
both patterns simultaneously, although @fig-sacwt-acf only shows the trend
pattern (try increasing the number of lags to see the seasonality pattern;
remember that a year has approximately $24 \times 365.25$ hours).


### Partial Autocorrelations

Autocorrelations alone don't give us a complete picture of the correlation
structure in time series.

To understand the problem, consider a series with just three observations:
$y_1, y_2, y_3$. If the lag-1 autocorrelation is large, then $y_1$ is
correlated with $y_2$, and $y_2$ is correlated with $y_3$. When we examine the
lag-2 autocorrelation, the correlation between $y_1$ and $y_3$, the
observations might be correlated on their own, or they might be correlated
because both are correlated with $y_2$. In other words, lag-1 autocorrelation
affects lag-2 autocorrelation, and for longer series, this problem applies to
all autocorrelations.

To overcome the problem, we also examine **partial autocorrelation**, which is
the autocorrelation *after removing the effects of observations at intermediary
lags*.

In R, the `PACF` function in the feasts package computes partial
autocorrelations for a tsibble. The syntax is the same as for the `ACF`
function.

The partial autocorrelations for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series
are:

```{r}
hood_pacf = PACF(hood, temp_f, lag_max = 24*5)
head(hood_pacf)
```

Once again we can use the `autoplot` function to make a **partial
autocorelation plot**, which shows lags on the x-axis and partial
autocorrelations on the y-axis:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-pacf
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Partial autocorrelation plot for the Sacramento River Water Temperature
#|    dataset.
autoplot(hood_pacf)
```

When a time series has seasonality, the partial autocorrelation tends to spike
at the lag approximately equal to the seasonal period. Using partial
autocorrelations to detect trend is difficult; use a plot of the series, a
decomposition, or autocorrelations instead.

@fig-sacwt-pacf shows large partial autocorrelations at lag-1 and perhaps
lag-2. All of the others shown are below 0.1.


## Stationary Series

A time series is **stationary** if the distribution at each time step doesn't
depend on the time. A series with trend or seasonality is never stationary. For
instance, the Sacramento River Water Temperature series is clearly not
stationary based on @fig-sacwt-line and @fig-sacwt-stl-periodic.

Visually, a stationary series displays no trend or seasonality, and the
variance is constant (the fluctuations do not become noticeably smaller or
larger over some time intervals). The [ARIMA Models][fpp-arima] chapter of
_Forecasting: Principles and Practices_, 3rd edition [@hyndman2021] provides
several plots of stationary and non-stationary time series.

For a stationary series, the autocorrelations either decrease to zero rapidly
or are all close to zero. Because of this, we'll often use autocorrelation
plots to help us assess whether a series is stationary.

:::{.callout-note title="Note: Portmanteau Tests"}
There are several hypothesis tests designed to test whether the
autocorrelations for a series are (mostly) zero, as we'd expect of a stationary
series. These are collectively known as **portmanteau tests** because they test
many autocorrelations at once. The **Ljung-Box test** is one of the most
widely-used portmanteau tests.

These tests tend to be highly sensitive to sample size, and will almost always
reject (which indicates the series is non-stationary) for time series with many
observations.
:::

When we fit a forecasting model (@sec-ts-forecasting), as a diagnostic we can
check that the residuals (for predictions of the training data) are stationary.
If they're not, then the model fails to capture some of the patterns in the
series and a better model may exist.

Some forecasting models (such as ARIMA; see @sec-ts-forecasting) assume the
time series being forecasted is stationary. There are a few things we can do to
transform a non-stationary series into a stationary series.

If the variance is not constant, taking the logarithm or a power of the series
will often stabilize it.

:::{.callout-note}
Logarithm and powe transformations are sometimes called **Box-Cox
transformations** because they can be written in a more general form. There are
automated methods to choose the best Box-Cox transformation for a series,
although it's still prudent to manually inspect the transformed series.
:::

If a series has trend or seasonality, we have several options for forecasting.
One approach is to decompose the series to remove the trend and seasonality,
check that the remainder is stationary, and then forecast on the remainder. The
remainder forecast can be combined with the trend and seasonal components to
get a forecast for the series.

Let's examine the remainder from the STL decomposition in
@sec-ts-stl-decomposition to check for stationarity. First, we'll make a time
versus feature plot. @fig-sacwt-stl-periodic showed a few extreme values; we'll
remove those to make patterns easier to see:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-stl-remainder
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Line plot of time versus temperature for the remainder component from the
#|    STL decomposition of the Sacramento River Water Temperature series, with
#|    extreme values (below -10 or above 10) removed.
autoplot(stl_cmp, remainder) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_minor_breaks = "1 year") +
  ylim(-10, 10)  #
```

The remainder series appears to have (mostly) constant variance and no trend in
@fig-sacwt-stl-remainder. Even with the extreme values removed, it's difficult
to tell from the figure whether there's any seasonality.

Now let's check the autocorrelation plot:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-stl-remainder-acf
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Autocorrelation plot for the remainder component from the STL
#|    decomposition of the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.
autoplot(ACF(stl_cmp, remainder, lag_max = 24*5))
```

@fig-sacwt-stl-remainder-acf shows large autocorrelations at all of the lags in
the plot. The remainder series is clearly not stationary. If we want to use it
for forecasting, we'll need to choose a method that doesn't require a
stationary series.

Another approach to forecasting a non-stationary series is to take
**differences**. In particular, take the series and subtract (or divide by) a
lagged copy of the series. Differencing at lag-1 works well for many series,
although if we have more context about the series, we may want to use a
different lag. For instance, differencing at lag equal to the seasonal period
can help remove seasonality. Occasionally, we might need to difference a series
several times to get something stationary. After taking differences, we can
check for stationarity, and then forecast on the differences.

Let's try taking differences of the remainder series from the STL decomposition
of the Sacramento River Water Temperature series. We can use the tsibble
package's `difference` function to do so:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-stl-remainder-diff-acf
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Autocorrelation plot for the first differences of the remainder component
#|    from the STL decomposition of the Sacramento River Water Temperature
#|    dataset.
autoplot(ACF(stl_cmp, difference(remainder, 1), lag_max = 24*5))
```

The autocorrelations for the differenced remainder series
(@fig-sacwt-stl-remainder-diff-acf) are much smaller than the autocorrelations
for the original remainder series (@fig-sacwt-stl-remainder-acf). Almost all of
the autocorrelations except the lag-1 and lag-3 are smaller than 0.05. The
largest, at lag-1, is only about -0.2. Although the differenced remainder
series isn't a perfect example of a stationary series, it might be okay to use
it with a forecasting model that requires stationarity. If we do, we can check
that the residuals are approximately stationary; this is a more important
diagnostic.


## Forecasting {#sec-ts-forecasting}

As with decomposition, there are many different methods for forecasting or
predicting future values of a time series. This section introduces just a few
of the most well-known methods.

There are also many different R packages for forecasting, as we hinted at in
@sec-ts-time-series-r. See that section for links to comprehensive guides. In
this section, we'll mostly use the [fable][] package to fit forecasting models.
Like the feasts package (from @sec-ts-stl-decomposition), the fable package
uses the generic `model` function to fit models. The package also uses the
generic `forecast` function to generate forecasts from fitted models.

[fable]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.fable

Forecasting models tend to be computationally demanding. Forecasting on a time
series with a large number of observations sometimes requires a lot of time and
memory. To ensure that the examples in this section will run on the average
laptop, we'll subset the Sacramento River Water Temperature series down to just
the final two years (2023-2024). Instead of filtering the dataset directly,
we'll use the components tsibble from the STL decomposition
(@sec-ts-stl-decomposition), since that contains the original data as well as
the components, which we might use later:

```{r}
hood23 = filter(stl_cmp, year(time) >= 2023)

# Remove the `.model` column, since it causes problems for downstream modeling:
hood23 = select(hood23, -.model)

head(hood23)
```

### Simple Methods

There are several relatively simple methods for forecasting:

* **Naive** forecasting: use the most recent observation for all forecasts. In
  fable, this is the `NAIVE` model function.
* **Seasonal naive** forecasting: use the corresponding observation from the
  previous seasonal period for each forecast. In fable, this is the `SNAIVE`
  model function.
* **Mean** forecasting: use the mean of the series for all forecasts. In fable,
  this is the `MEAN` model function.
* **Drift** forecasting: use the line that passes through the first and last
  observation for all forecasts. In fable, this is the `DRIFT` model function.

Let's try forecasting for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series with
the naive method. First, we fit the model with the `model` function:

```{r}
library("fable")

naive_fit = model(hood23, naive = NAIVE(temp_f))
```

Next, we forecast with the `forecast` function (see `?forecast.mdl_df` for
help). Use the `h` parameter to set the number of forecasts. In this case,
we'll forecast the next 3 days:

```{r}
naive_fcst = forecast(naive_fit, h = 24*3)
```

We can plot the forecasts with the `autoplot` function, adding an `autolayer`
to also show the original series:

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-sacwt-fcst-naive
#| fig-cap: >
#|    7-day naive forecasts for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.
lims = tail(hood23$time, 1) + days(c(-29, 7))

autoplot(naive_fcst) +
  autolayer(hood23, temp_f) +
  xlim(lims)
```

The forecasts (@fig-sacwt-fcst-naive) are automatically plotted with prediction
intervals. Since we used the naive method, all of the forecasts are the same.
The prediction intervals get wider at times farther into the future to indicate
increasing uncertainty about the forecasts.

:::{.callout-tip}
To extract the prediction intervals as numbers, use the `hilo` function. See
`?forecast.mdl_df` and `?hilo` for more details.
:::

As one more example, since this series exhibits strong seasonality, let's
forecast with the seasonal naive method. For this method, we must specify the
length of the seasonal period with a model formula and the special `lag`
function:

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-sacwt-fcst-snaive
#| fig-cap: >
#|    7-day seasonal naive forecasts for the Sacramento River Water Temperature
#|    dataset, where the seasonal period is 1 year.
snaive_fit = model(hood23, snaive = SNAIVE(temp_f ~ lag("1y")))
snaive_fcst = forecast(snaive_fit, h = 24*3)

autoplot(snaive_fcst) +
  autolayer(hood23, temp_f) +
  xlim(lims)
```

The forecasts in @fig-sacwt-fcst-snaive vary over time since the seasonal naive
method takes observations from the previous season as forecasts. This is also
why the prediction intervals have constant width and are wider than in
@fig-sacwt-fcst-naive; the forecasts are not necessarily better closer to the
most recent observation.

Although the methods described in this section are simple, they often work
surprisingly well. They're also easy to interpret. For series with strong
seasonal components, these methods can be improved without much additional
complexity by decomposing the series, forecasting on the remainder series, and
then recombining the forecasts with the seasonal components.


### Linear Models

Linear models are especially useful for forecasting time series when there are
meaningful predictors available, as is often the case for multivariate time
series. Regardless of whether the time series is multivariate, linear models
can be effective at modeling simple trends and relatively complex seasonality.

In fable, the model function for a linear model is `TSLM`. The function
requires a model formula (just like the `lm` function). The model formula
can include several special functions, such as:

* `trend` to include a linear time trend.
* `season` to include a categorical predictors for seasonality. The seasonal
  period must be specified. This creates one predictor for each time step
  (except the first) in the seasonal period, so it's not recommended for long
  seasonal periods.
* `fourier` to include Fourier predictors for seasonality. The seasonal period
  must be specified, and the number of predictors can optionally be specified.
  Fourier predictors are sine and cosine functions of time; just a few Fourier
  predictors can approximate most seasonal patterns well. Fourier predictors
  are appropriate to use even for long seasonal periods.

See `?common_xregs` for a complete list of special functions.

Let's fit a linear model to the Sacramento River Water Temperature series.
We'll include Fourier terms for 1-year and 1-day seasonality. Since linear
models handle trend and seasonality reasonably well, we'll forecast 1 year into
the future:

```{r}
tslm_fit = model(
  hood23,
  lm = TSLM(
    temp_f ~ trend() + fourier(24*365, 5) + fourier(24, 3)
  )
)

report(tslm_fit)
```

:::{.callout-tip}
The fable package's `report` function provides a summary of a model fitted with
`model` (similar to the output from `summary` for a model fitted with `lm`).
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-fcst-linear-fourier
#| fig-cap: >
#|    1-year linear model forecasts for the Sacramento River Water Temperature
#|    dataset, with Fourier terms for 1-year and 24-hour seasonality.
tslm_fcst = forecast(tslm_fit, h = 24*365)

autoplot(tslm_fcst) +
  autolayer(hood23, temp_f)
```

@fig-sacwt-fcst-linear-fourier shows the forecasts and associated prediction
intervals. For a linear model, the prediction intervals are estimated based on
the variance of the residuals (this is true for any linear model, not just in
the time series context).


### ARIMA Models

An autoregressive integrated moving average model, or **ARIMA model**, is a
combination of three simpler methods:

1. An **autoregressive model**, denoted AR($p$) assumes each observation is a
   linear combination of the previous $p$ observations and an error term.

   The simplest AR model, denoted AR(1), uses only 1 previous observation.
   Mathematically, for an observation $y_t$ and error term $\epsilon_t$, the
   model is

   $$
   y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \epsilon_t
   $$

   The model estimates the values of the coefficients $c$ and $\phi_1$.

2. Integrated (I) refers to differencing, which is built into ARIMA models. The
   order of differencing is denoted by $d$.

3. A **moving average model**, denoted MA($q$) assumes each observation is a
   linear combination of the previous $q$ error terms and a new error term.

   The simplest MA model, denoted MA(1), uses only 1 previous error term.
   Mathematically, for an observation $y_t$ and error term $\epsilon_t$, the
   model is

   $$
   y_t = c + \theta_1 \epsilon_{t-1} + \epsilon_t
   $$

   The model estimates the values of the coefficients $c$ and $\theta_1$.

ARIMA models are denoted by ARIMA($p$, $d$, $q$) to indicate the parameters for
the three methods.

:::{.callout-warning}
AR, MA, and ARIMA models all assume a stationary time series.

They will not necessarily work well for a series that isn't stationary, and the
estimated standard errors and prediction intervals will not be correct.

There is an extension of ARIMA for time series with seasonality (but not
trend). The `ARIMA` model function (explained and demonstrated below) will
automatically consider seasonal ARIMA models.
:::

In fable, the model function for an ARIMA model is `ARIMA`. The function
requires one argument: a feature to model or a model formula. With a model
formula, we use the special `pdq` function to manually set the parameters $p$,
$d$, and $q$. When these are not specified, fable will automatically try to
find the best settings by fitting and comparing multiple models.

Let's try fitting an ARIMA model to the almost-stationary remainder component
from the STL decomposition (@sec-ts-stl-decomposition) of the Sacramento River
Water Temperature series. We'll let fable select the best model automatically:

```{r}
arima_fit = model(hood23, arima = ARIMA(remainder))
report(arima_fit)
```

In this case, the best model was an ARIMA(1, 0, 4) model with a seasonal
ARIMA(1, 1, 0) model for a 24-hour seasonal period.

Let's use the model to forecast 1 year into the future:

```{r}
#| label: fig-sacwt-fcst-arima
#| fig-cap: >
#|    1-year ARIMA forecasts for the remainder component from the STL
#|    decomposition of the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.
arima_fcst = forecast(arima_fit, h = 24*365)

autoplot(arima_fcst) +
  autolayer(hood23, remainder)
```

Judging from @fig-sacwt-fcst-arima, it seems like the ARIMA model doesn't fit
well. While the forecasts do fluctuate slightly, they don't appear to be that
much different from the naive method or the mean method, despite the much more
complicated model. This may be due to the lack of stationarity in the remainder
series.

:::{.callout-warning}
For any model, examining the residuals is critical for determining how well the
model fits and whether its assumptions are satisfied.

The `resid` function returns the residuals as a tsibble for an fable model.

The ggtime package's `gg_tsresiduals` function makes diagnostic plots for a
time series model. These include a time versus feature plot, autocorrelation
plot, and histogram for the residuals.
:::

:::{.callout-tip}
When forecasting is the primary goal, estimates of forecast accuracy are
usually the best way to compare models.

We can estimate forecast accuracy by partitioning the time series into a
training series and a testing series. Use only the training series to fit
models, then forecast on the testing series to evaluate the models. The
simplest way to do this is to treat (approximately) the first 80% of the series
as training and the remaining 20% as testing. There are other, more
sophisticated ways to partition time series into training and testing series
that address specific limitations of this simple approach.
:::

:::{.callout-note title="See Also"}
There are many, many other kinds of decomposition and forecasting models!

The textbook [_Forecasting: Principles and Practice_, 3rd Edition][fpp3]
[@hyndman2021] is a good starting point for learning about more models. It also
explains the statistics and algorithm fable uses to compare different ARIMA
models.
:::
